common_name: American Golden Russet Apple (Bronze-Skinned Pre-1800 Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; American Golden Russet dates to before 1800 and was grown across the South for its sugary juice prized fresh, dried, and pressed for cider, so plant a second apple cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, spacing standard trees 12-20 feet apart for mature canopy spread. American Golden Russet is a pre-1800 American heirloom with rusty, bronze-gold skin and yellow, crisp, aromatic flesh that produces exceptionally sugary juice, making it a favorite for fresh eating, drying, and cider pressing. Fruit is medium or smaller, ripening September through October, and the tree is a reliable, moderately vigorous grower well suited to Southern orchards. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation.
sources: Century Farm Orchards
Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples

common_name: American Summer Pearmain Apple (1817 Southern Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; first described in 1817 and grown throughout the South on a wide range of soils, American Summer Pearmain ripens unevenly over several weeks, so plan on repeated picking rather than a single harvest, and site a pollinizer nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained fertile soil in full sun. American Summer Pearmain was first described in 1817 and was widely planted across the South, earning high marks for exceptional eating quality; fruit is medium to large, greenish-yellow with red stripes, ripening gradually over roughly four weeks between July and August, which makes it well suited for both fresh eating and drying since not all fruit matures at once. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby, as it is not reliably self-fruitful, and prune in late winter to keep the canopy open in humid Southern summers.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, giving the fast-growing tree room to develop its naturally strong, easily-pruned limb structure. Aunt Rachel is a North Carolina Piedmont heirloom, originating in Chatham County and passed down through local families; fruit is red with darker stripes over white, firm flesh that is mildly tart and juicy, good for both fresh eating and cooking. The tree shows better-than-average disease resistance for an older Southern heirloom, and fruit ripens in late July into early August. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby for best fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Bevan's Favorite was first described in 1859 and was valued across the South for ripening early, around early to mid-July, well ahead of most other apples. common_name: Father Abraham Apple (Pre-1755 Southern Keeper and Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; Father Abraham originated before 1755, possibly in South Carolina, and is valued as a late-ripening apple that stores well and makes excellent cider, so site a pollinizer apple nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Father Abraham is one of the oldest documented Southern apples, dating to before 1755 and possibly originating in South Carolina; it is a late-ripening variety harvested from late October into November, prized historically for long storage and for making excellent cider. Fruit is medium to small, dull red, fine-grained, and ranges from sweet to slightly acidic. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby and store fruit in a cool root cellar to extend its keeping season through winter.

common_name: Johnson Keeper Apple (Johnson's Red Winter, Mississippi Heirloom)

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, in a site suited to the warmer Deep South given its Mississippi origin. Johnson Keeper is an attractive, slightly flattened apple ripening in late October to early November, sweet, juicy, and firm, with excellent storage qualities that historically kept fruit edible into spring without refrigeration. It is thought to be the same apple once known as Johnson's Red Winter, believed extinct before being rediscovered. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby and store ripe fruit in a cool, dark root cellar for maximum keeping time.

common_name: Keener Seedling Apple (Lincoln County North Carolina Russet Heirloom)

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Keener Seedling is a North Carolina Piedmont heirloom originating in Lincoln County around 1880, heavily russeted with a slight red blush over medium-sized fruit with white, sweet, firm flesh. The tree is disease resistant and the fruit ripens extremely late in the season, often hanging on the tree into late November, making it one of the last Southern heirlooms harvested each year. Fruit is good for fresh eating, cooking, and long storage. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby for consistent fruit set.

It is a good all-purpose apple for fresh eating, excellent for cooking, and dries well, ripening over an extended window from late July into early September. directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Red Rebel is a Virginia heirloom originating around 1850 in Rappahannock County that was nearly extinct before being rediscovered in the 1980s; an 1908 USDA report singled out its fine appearance and dessert quality as worth further testing. The tree is highly disease resistant and produces beautiful, symmetrical, medium to large deep red apples with firm white flesh that is mildly sweet. Fruit ripens in mid-September and stores into December under refrigeration. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby for reliable fruit set.

Flesh is moderately firm, white, juicy, and mildly subacid, and the tree shows good disease resistance. Fruit ripens early to mid-July. common_name: Yellow June Apple (Known Since 1845 Early-Season Southern Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow June has been known since 1845 with origin otherwise unrecorded, ripening June into early July as one of the very first Southern apples of the season, so site a pollinizer apple nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Yellow June has been documented since 1845, with its original origin otherwise unrecorded, and is prized as one of the very first apples to ripen each year, typically in June and often around the Father's Day timeframe in the South. Flavor is tart and considered one of the best among frying apples, though fruit bruises easily and does not keep well, so plan to use it fresh or cooked shortly after picking. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby, and harvest promptly since the fruit does not store.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun in the cool upland sites where Limbertwig strains perform best. Swiss Limbertwig traces back to Swiss settlers in the Cumberland Mountains of Tennessee and Kentucky, producing red fruit marked with conspicuous large white dots over firm, sweet, very crisp flesh. It ripens in October and, like other Limbertwig strains, develops its best flavor in cooler mountain climates. Provide a compatible pollinizer apple nearby, since like most Limbertwig strains it is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on the cool upland sites favored by Limbertwig strains. Red Limbertwig, also called Old Fashioned Limbertwig, is sweeter in flavor than many other named Limbertwig strains, producing red, firm fruit with good keeping qualities that ripens extremely late, typically in November. Like other Limbertwig apples it is best adapted to Southern Appalachian mountain and upper Piedmont climates where cool nights help develop its flavor.
